n: After the side note on Esau, the story returns to Jacob, living as a sojourner in Canaan just as Isaac had. The covenant land was promised, but not yet possessed.

f.g: a resident foreigner, living in the land without owning it

n: The long story of Joseph begins. At seventeen he worked with his half-brothers and reported their bad behavior to Jacob, which did not make him popular.

f.g: Hebrew toledot — “family history”; this one runs to the end of Genesis.
a bad account of their conduct

n: Jacob openly favored Joseph, the first son of his beloved Rachel, and gave him a special robe that marked him as the favored heir.

f.g: Hebrew ketonet passim — perhaps a long-sleeved or richly ornamented robe; a sign of rank.

n: Favoritism bred resentment. The brothers’ hatred grew so strong they could not even greet Joseph kindly—a warning about how envy poisons families.

f.g: could not even say “shalom” (peace) to him

n: Joseph shared a dream with his brothers, and it only deepened their hatred. In Genesis dreams are often a way God reveals the future.
Joseph eagerly asks them to listen. His youthful openness may have been naïve, but the dream itself was from God.

f.g: please

n: In the dream the brothers’ bundles of grain bowed to Joseph’s. Fittingly, it would be grain that later brought them to Egypt to bow before him.

f.g: bowed down in respect
bundles of cut grain

n: The brothers understood the meaning at once: Joseph would rule over them. Their questions drip with scorn, and their hatred grew.

f.w: Shalt thou indeed reign over us?

n: A second dream widened the picture: sun, moon, and eleven stars—his father, mother, and eleven brothers—bowed to him.

f.w: the sun and the moon and the eleven stars

n: Even Jacob scolded Joseph, asking whether the whole family would bow to him. The mention of “thy mother” is striking since Rachel had died; it may be symbolic of the whole household.

f.g: scolded, corrected

n: The brothers seethed with jealousy, but Jacob quietly kept the dream in mind, sensing it might mean something—much as Mary later pondered things in her heart.

f.g: kept the matter in mind

n: The brothers took the flocks about fifty miles north to Shechem, where good pasture was—and where they had earlier massacred the city’s men.
Jacob sends Joseph to check on them, and Joseph answers with readiness: “Here am I,” the same humble response of Abraham and later prophets.
Joseph is sent on a simple errand of peace—to ask after his brothers’ welfare—yet it begins his journey to Egypt. God often works through ordinary tasks.

f.w: see whether it be well with thy brethren
f.g: literally “see the shalom (peace, welfare) of your brothers”

n: A nameless man finds Joseph wandering. This small encounter keeps the story moving; without it Joseph might have gone home.
Joseph simply says he is looking for his brothers—an ironic line, since they are about to reject him.
The brothers had moved on to Dothan, about 15 miles north, along a trade route to Egypt—which sets up what happens next.

f.g: a town on the caravan road from Gilead to Egypt

n: Spotting the hated robe from far away, the brothers plotted murder before Joseph even arrived.

f.g: plotted together

n: They mock him as “this dreamer”—literally “master of dreams.” Their contempt is aimed at the very gift God gave him.

f.g: Hebrew “this lord of dreams,” a sneer

n: Their plan: kill him, hide the body in a cistern, and blame a wild animal. They intend to destroy his dreams—but they will end up fulfilling them.

f.g: a cistern dug to store rainwater

f.w: we shall see what will become of his dreams

n: Reuben, the oldest, stepped in to stop the killing. Perhaps he hoped to regain his father’s trust after his earlier sin.
Reuben proposed throwing Joseph into a dry cistern instead, secretly planning to rescue him and bring him home.
The first thing they did was strip off the robe that symbolized their father’s favor. Joseph will later be stripped of a garment again in Potiphar’s house.

f.g: stripped

n: The cistern was dry, so Joseph would not drown—but he could not climb out. Being thrown into a pit is a biblical picture of deep distress.

f.w: there was no water in it

n: Coldly, the brothers sat down to eat while Joseph cried below. A trading caravan appeared, carrying valuable resins and spices to Egypt.

f.g: Ishmaelites—traders descended from Ishmael
a healing resin; Gilead was famous for it
fragrant resin used in perfume and burial

n: Judah asks what they gain by murder. His argument is practical more than moral, but it saves Joseph’s life.
Judah suggests selling Joseph instead—“he is our brother.” It is a half-step toward conscience; Judah’s full change comes later.

f.g: our own family, our blood relative
agreed

n: Joseph was sold for twenty pieces of silver, roughly the price of a slave in that era. Christians have long seen a parallel in Jesus being sold for thirty pieces.

f.g: The trader names Ishmaelite and Midianite seem to overlap here.

n: Reuben, who had been away, came back to find the pit empty. Tearing clothing was a sign of intense grief.

f.g: tore his clothes in mourning

n: Reuben cries that the boy is gone—and as oldest son he feels responsible for facing his father.

f.g: the boy is gone

n: The brothers use a goat’s blood to fake Joseph’s death. Jacob, who once deceived his father with goat skins and Esau’s garment, is now deceived the same way.
They hand the bloody robe to Jacob and ask him to “recognize” it—a cruel way of avoiding a direct lie.

f.g: Hebrew “recognize”—a key word that returns in Genesis 38:25.

n: Jacob recognized the robe and drew the conclusion they intended: Joseph had been torn apart by a wild animal.
Jacob mourned with the customary signs: torn clothes and sackcloth, a rough goat-hair cloth worn in grief.

f.g: coarse cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance

n: No one could console Jacob; he expected to grieve until death. The brothers’ secret now burdens the whole family for over twenty years.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead

n: Meanwhile, Joseph arrived in Egypt and was sold to Potiphar, a high royal official. The narrator hints that God’s plan is quietly unfolding.

f.g: an Egyptian name meaning roughly “he whom Ra gave”
possibly chief of the royal bodyguard or executioners
